## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Sub-Pixel Image Processing
  Official title       Sub-pixel image processing
  Instructors          L. MOISAN (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 1 · period 1 (28/09/2026 – 08/01/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 36 h (lectures 20 h, labs 16 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Modelling]{.badge .label} · domains on master-mva.com: Image processing
  Language             not displayed on the official pages (the master-mva.com course description is written in English)
  Assessment           Exam (master-mva.com, “Mode de validation”); the Université Paris-Saclay course detail states “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale” (continuous assessment that is not the only component of the grade); no weighting displayed
  Prerequisites        Basics of Fourier analysis and differential calculus (master-mva.com, “Prè-requis”)
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with a good M1 in applied mathematics, computer science or physics who knows the Fourier transform and wants image algorithms that stay exact at the scale of a fraction of a pixel.

**Empirical first**: rotate a test image 36 times by 10° with bilinear interpolation and the full turn leaves it visibly blurred (an RMS error of 5.1 grey levels for an image of RMS 12, Code 3.11); the same full turn computed with FFT-based shears returns it to within $4 \times 10^{-8}$. A striped shirt photographed with a phone shows moiré for a related reason: frequencies above the sensor's Nyquist limit fold back as false patterns.

A digital image is an array of numbers, but the scene, the optics and most image-processing models are continuous. This course builds the bridge in both directions. It explains which continuous image the pixels are samples of, how to turn a continuous operation (a translation, a rotation, a derivative, a diffusion) into an exact or controlled discrete algorithm, and how to read geometry from pixels at a precision far below the grid step.

The tools are Fourier analysis, sampling theory, splines and a little probability. They reappear in [Mathematical Models for Digital Photography](../s1-digital-photography/index.html), [Image Denoising](../s1-image-denoising/index.html), [Inverse Problems and Imaging](../s2-inverse-problems-imaging/index.html), [Remote Sensing Data](../s2-remote-sensing/index.html) and [Generative Models for Images](../s2-generative-models-images/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Model the acquisition chain of a digital image — projection, diffraction, pixel integration, sampling and noise — and predict where it aliases.
-   State and prove the Poisson summation formula and the Shannon–Whittaker theorem, and bound the error made when an image is not band-limited.
-   Implement exact sub-pixel translations and zooms with the FFT, including the delicate Nyquist coefficient of even sizes.
-   Remove the border artefacts of the DFT with the periodic plus smooth decomposition.
-   Build spline interpolators by prefiltering and compare interpolators through their frequency responses.
-   Rotate images losslessly with three FFT-based shears, and explain why bilinear interpolation cannot do this.
-   Choose a prefilter for image reduction by quantifying the aliasing, ringing and blur it produces.
-   Design consistent, isotropic discrete derivatives and stable iterative filters, from the heat equation to curvature flows.
-   Estimate translations, edges and shapes with sub-pixel accuracy, and compare the result with the Cramér–Rao bound.
-   Use the phase spectrum to synthesise micro-textures and to compute phase-based sharpness indices.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com sets the objective of exploring ways, and applications, of linking continuous and discrete image models. It asks two questions: how to translate a continuous image-processing model into a discrete numerical algorithm, and, conversely, how to extract geometric information from a discrete array of pixels.

The same page announces sessions split half into lectures and half into exercise or computer practice, and an exam. Its two references are L. Moisan's lecture notes *Modeling and Image Processing* and his 2011 paper on the periodic plus smooth image decomposition, both available on the course web page. The official prerequisites are the basics of Fourier analysis and differential calculus.

-   **Related courses of the same semester** — [Mathematical Models for Digital Photography](../s1-digital-photography/index.html) (camera pipeline, noise, demosaicking), [Image Denoising](../s1-image-denoising/index.html), [3D Computer Vision](../s1-3d-computer-vision/index.html) (pinhole geometry, homographies, stereo), [The Machine Intelligence of Images](../s1-machine-intelligence-images/index.html) and [Medical Image Analysis Based on Generative, Geometric and Biophysical Models](../s1-medical-image-analysis/index.html).
-   **Courses that build on it (semester 2)** — [Inverse Problems and Imaging](../s2-inverse-problems-imaging/index.html) (deconvolution, sampling models), [Generative Models for Images](../s2-generative-models-images/index.html) (texture synthesis), [Deep Learning for Image Restoration and Synthesis](../s2-dl-image-restoration-synthesis/index.html), [Remote Sensing Data](../s2-remote-sensing/index.html) (satellite sampling, sub-pixel registration), [Deformable Models and Geodesic Methods](../s2-deformable-models-geodesics/index.html) and [Audio Signal Processing: Time–Frequency Analysis](../s2-audio-time-frequency/index.html) (the same Fourier tools in one dimension).

### Course outline

-   **Review: Fourier analysis and differential calculus** — the Fourier transform, the Poisson summation formula, the DFT and the curvature of level lines.
-   **The image formation process** — pinhole geometry, diffraction, pixel integration, sampling, aliasing and noise, combined into one acquisition model.
-   **Shannon sampling and Fourier interpolation** — the Shannon–Whittaker theorem, the interpolation of finite images by the DFT, exact translations and zooms, and the periodic plus smooth decomposition.
-   **Splines and lossless geometric transforms** — interpolation kernels, B-splines and prefiltering, frequency responses, and rotations by three FFT shears.
-   **Image reduction: aliasing, ringing and blur** — three measures of the defects of a prefilter, the Gibbs overshoot, and a theorem showing that no positive filter escapes the trade-off.
-   **Differential operators and iterative filtering** — consistency and isotropy of discrete derivatives, stability of the heat equation, curvature motion.
-   **Sub-pixel image geometry** — registration at the Cramér–Rao bound, phase correlation, peak and edge localisation, level lines.
-   **The phase spectrum: textures and sharpness** — what the phase carries, random phase textures, and the phase-coherence sharpness index.
-   **Research directions and open problems** — self-study: Shannon-consistent variational models, aliasing in neural networks, continuous representations, super-resolution.

### How to study this module

-   Read [ch. 0](#ch0) before the first session even if Fourier analysis feels familiar: the conventions fixed there ($2\pi$ in the exponent, angular frequencies, unnormalised DFT) are used everywhere afterwards.
-   Run every code block and change one parameter at a time; the numbers quoted in the text were produced by these blocks. They need Python 3 with NumPy, SciPy and Matplotlib (the level-line extraction of [ch. 6](#ch6) uses `contourpy`, which Matplotlib installs).
-   Experiment with odd image sizes first, where the FFT tools are exactly invertible; then study the even case ([ch. 2.3–2.4](#ch2), Exercise 7).
-   Do the exercises listed for each session before the next one; the ★★ proofs of [ch. 2](#ch2), 4 and 5 are typical exam questions.
-   Keep two test images throughout the course: a smooth, well-sampled one and a sharp, aliased one. Most phenomena of the course appear as a difference between the two.

## 0. Review: Fourier analysis and differential calculus {#ch0}

Every chapter of the course moves between a continuous image and its samples. This review fixes the conventions of the Fourier transform, proves the one identity that links the two worlds (the Poisson summation formula), and recalls the differential geometry of level lines used in [ch. 5](#ch5) and [ch. 6](#ch6).

### 0.1 The Fourier transform

We use angular frequencies, so that the sampling grid $\mathbb{Z}^d$ corresponds to the frequency band $[-\pi, \pi]^d$.

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Fourier transform]{.tag} For $f \in L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)$, the Fourier transform of $f$ is the bounded continuous function
$$
\hat f(\xi) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} f(x)\, e^{-i \langle x, \xi \rangle}\, dx, \qquad \xi \in \mathbb{R}^d .
$$

When $\hat f$ is also integrable, the inversion formula holds at every point of continuity of $f$:
$$
f(x) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^d} \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \hat f(\xi)\, e^{i \langle x, \xi \rangle}\, d\xi .
$$

The transform extends to $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, where Plancherel's identity reads
$$
\int |f|^2 = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^d} \int |\hat f|^2 .
$$
:::

The rules below are used without comment in the rest of the page. Each one follows from a change of variables or an integration by parts in the definition.

| Operation | Function | Fourier transform |
|---|---|---|
| translation | $f(x - a)$ | $e^{-i\langle a, \xi\rangle} \hat f(\xi)$ |
| modulation | $e^{i \langle \eta, x \rangle} f(x)$ | $\hat f(\xi - \eta)$ |
| dilation ($\lambda > 0$) | $f(x / \lambda)$ | $\lambda^d \hat f(\lambda \xi)$ |
| convolution | $f * g$ | $\hat f\, \hat g$ |
| derivative | $\partial_j f$ | $i \xi_j \hat f(\xi)$ |
| Gaussian density, variance $\sigma^2$ per axis | $g_\sigma(x)$ | $e^{-\sigma^2 \lvert\xi\rvert^2 / 2}$ |
| box (1D) | $\mathbf{1}_{[-1/2, 1/2]}(x)$ | $\frac{\sin(\xi/2)}{\xi/2}$ |
| cardinal sine (1D) | $\mathrm{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin \pi x}{\pi x}$ | $\mathbf{1}_{[-\pi, \pi]}(\xi)$ |

Two facts matter for imaging. First, a convolution — blur, pixel integration, any linear shift-invariant filter — acts frequency by frequency as a multiplication. Second, a translation changes only the *phase* of the transform, never its modulus; [ch. 6](#ch6) and [ch. 7](#ch7) exploit this.

### 0.2 Fourier series and the Poisson summation formula

A 1-periodic function $F$ that is regular enough is the sum of its Fourier series. Its coefficients are
$$
c_m(F) = \int_0^1 F(x)\, e^{-2 i \pi m x}\, dx, \qquad F(x) = \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} c_m(F)\, e^{2 i \pi m x} .
$$

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.2 — Poisson summation formula]{.tag} Let $f$ belong to the Schwartz class $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$. Then, for every $x \in \mathbb{R}$,
$$
\sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} f(x + k) = \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} \hat f(2\pi m)\, e^{2 i \pi m x} .
$$

Equivalently, for every frequency $\xi \in \mathbb{R}$, the samples of $f$ satisfy
$$
\sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} f(k)\, e^{-i k \xi} = \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} \hat f(\xi + 2\pi m) .
$$

::: proof
The left-hand side $F(x) = \sum_k f(x + k)$ converges uniformly with all its derivatives, so $F$ is smooth and 1-periodic.

Its Fourier coefficients are computed by exchanging sum and integral, then gluing the intervals $[k, k+1]$:
$$
c_m(F) = \sum_{k} \int_0^1 f(x + k)\, e^{-2 i \pi m x}\, dx = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(y)\, e^{-2 i \pi m y}\, dy = \hat f(2\pi m) .
$$

A smooth periodic function equals its Fourier series everywhere, which gives the first identity.

For the second one, apply the first at $x = 0$ to the function $f_\xi(y) = f(y)\, e^{-i y \xi}$, whose transform is $\hat f(\cdot + \xi)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key result — sampling periodises the spectrum]{.tag}
$$
\sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} f(k)\, e^{-i k \xi} = \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} \hat f(\xi + 2\pi m)
$$
:::

The second form is the heart of sampling theory. The left side is computed from the samples only; the right side is the spectrum of $f$ *periodised* with period $2\pi$. Sampling a function therefore superposes copies of its spectrum. The identity extends to $d$ dimensions with $\mathbb{Z}^d$ in place of $\mathbb{Z}$, by applying it variable by variable.

### 0.3 The discrete Fourier transform

::: def
[Definition 0.3 — Discrete Fourier transform (DFT)]{.tag} For a signal $u = (u_0, \dots, u_{M-1}) \in \mathbb{C}^M$, indices taken modulo $M$, the DFT is
$$
\hat u_p = \sum_{k=0}^{M-1} u_k\, e^{-2 i \pi p k / M}, \qquad u_k = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{p=0}^{M-1} \hat u_p\, e^{2 i \pi p k / M} .
$$

For an image $u$ of size $M \times N$, the 2D DFT applies the 1D transform along each axis. This is the convention of `numpy.fft`: unnormalised forward transform, factor $1/M$ in the inverse.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.4 — Properties of the DFT]{.tag} For $u, v \in \mathbb{C}^M$:

1.  Parseval: $\sum_k |u_k|^2 = \frac{1}{M} \sum_p |\hat u_p|^2$.
2.  Circular convolution: if $(u \circledast v)_k = \sum_j u_j v_{k - j}$, then $\widehat{u \circledast v} = \hat u\, \hat v$.
3.  Real signals: if $u$ is real, then $\hat u_{-p} = \overline{\hat u_p}$; the coefficients $\hat u_0$ and, for even $M$, $\hat u_{M/2}$ are real.
4.  Sampling of the spectrum: $\hat u_p = U(2\pi p / M)$, where $U(\xi) = \sum_k u_k e^{-ik\xi}$ is the discrete-time Fourier transform.

::: proof
All four follow from the orthogonality relation below, which is a finite geometric sum:
$$
\sum_{k=0}^{M-1} e^{2 i \pi (p - q) k / M} = M\, \mathbf{1}[p \equiv q \bmod M] .
$$

For item 2, expand $\widehat{u \circledast v}_p$ and substitute $k = j + l$; the sum factorises because indices are periodic. Items 3 and 4 are read directly on the definition. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The fast Fourier transform computes the DFT in $\mathcal{O}(M \log M)$ operations instead of $\mathcal{O}(M^2)$. Every "exact" algorithm of [ch. 2](#ch2) and [ch. 3](#ch3) costs a few FFTs.

The index $p$ should be read as a signed frequency. The coefficient $\hat u_p$ with $p > M/2$ describes the frequency $p - M$, and `numpy.fft.fftfreq` returns these signed values.

For even $M$, the coefficient $p = M/2$ is the *Nyquist* frequency, shared between $+M/2$ and $-M/2$; [ch. 2.3](#ch2) shows that it needs special care.

### 0.4 Differential calculus of level lines

An image $u : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ of class $C^2$ has gradient $\nabla u = (u_x, u_y)$ and Hessian $D^2 u$. Its *level lines* are the curves $\{u = \lambda\}$.

Where $\nabla u \neq 0$, the implicit function theorem says that the level line through a point is locally a $C^2$ curve, orthogonal to $\nabla u$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.5 — Curvature of a level line]{.tag} Let $u$ be $C^2$ near a point where $\nabla u \neq 0$. The curvature of the level line through that point is
$$
\mathrm{curv}(u) = \mathrm{div}\Big( \frac{\nabla u}{|\nabla u|} \Big) = \frac{u_{xx} u_y^2 - 2 u_{xy} u_x u_y + u_{yy} u_x^2}{|\nabla u|^3} .
$$

With this sign convention, a bright disc of radius $R$ on a dark background has curvature $-1/R$ on its boundary.

::: proof
Parametrise the level line by arc length, $s \mapsto \gamma(s)$. Differentiating $u(\gamma(s)) = \lambda$ once gives $\langle \nabla u, \gamma' \rangle = 0$, so the unit tangent is
$$
\gamma' = \frac{(-u_y, u_x)}{|\nabla u|} .
$$

Differentiating a second time gives
$$
D^2 u(\gamma', \gamma') + \langle \nabla u, \gamma'' \rangle = 0 .
$$

With $n = \nabla u / |\nabla u|$, this reads
$$
\langle \gamma'', n \rangle = - \frac{D^2 u(\gamma', \gamma')}{|\nabla u|} = - \frac{u_{xx} u_y^2 - 2 u_{xy} u_x u_y + u_{yy} u_x^2}{|\nabla u|^3} .
$$

The signed curvature is $-\langle \gamma'', n \rangle$, and expanding the divergence of $\nabla u / |\nabla u|$ gives the same expression.

For the disc, $n$ points towards the centre, as does $\gamma''$, with $|\gamma''| = 1/R$; hence the value $-1/R$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The numerator is $|\nabla u|^2$ times the second derivative of $u$ in the direction of the level line. Ch. 5.5 discretises it, and [ch. 6.5](#ch6) measures shapes from level lines.

**Code 0.6 — Checking the conventions.** The script verifies the Poisson summation formula on a Gaussian and the DFT conventions of NumPy.

```python
import numpy as np

# Poisson summation for a Gaussian: sum_k g(k) e^{-i k xi} = sum_m ghat(xi + 2 pi m)
s = 0.7                                   # standard deviation (pixels)
g = lambda x: np.exp(-x**2 / (2 * s**2)) / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi * s**2)
ghat = lambda xi: np.exp(-s**2 * xi**2 / 2)
k, m = np.arange(-60, 61), np.arange(-20, 21)
for xi in [0.0, 1.0, np.pi]:
    lhs = np.sum(g(k) * np.exp(-1j * k * xi)).real
    rhs = np.sum(ghat(xi + 2 * np.pi * m))
    print(f"xi = {xi:.3f}:  samples side {lhs:.10f}   periodized side {rhs:.10f}")

# DFT conventions of numpy: forward unnormalized, inverse with 1/M
u = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=8)
U = np.fft.fft(u)
print("Parseval:", np.allclose(np.sum(u**2), np.sum(abs(U)**2) / 8))
print("Hermitian symmetry:", np.allclose(U[1:], np.conj(U[1:][::-1])))
```

Both sides agree to ten digits at $\xi = 0$, $1$ and $\pi$.

Note the value at $\xi = 0$: the sum of the samples of a Gaussian of unit mass is $1.000126$, not $1$. The excess is the contribution of the spectral copies $\hat g(\pm 2\pi)$, a first glimpse of aliasing.

::: recap
[Key takeaways — chapter 0]{.tag}

-   The Fourier transform uses angular frequencies; the grid $\mathbb{Z}^d$ corresponds to the band $[-\pi, \pi]^d$.
-   Convolutions become products, translations change only the phase.
-   The Poisson summation formula says that sampling periodises the spectrum.
-   The DFT samples the spectrum of a finite signal; the Nyquist coefficient of even sizes is special.
-   The curvature of level lines is $\mathrm{div}(\nabla u / |\nabla u|)$, an expression in first and second derivatives.
:::

## 1. The image formation process {#ch1}

Before processing an image we need to know what its pixels measure. This chapter follows light from the scene to the sensor: the geometry of the projection, the blur imposed by diffraction, the integration over each photosite, the sampling on a grid, and the noise. The result is an acquisition model that the rest of the course inverts or exploits.

### 1.1 Geometry: the pinhole camera

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Pinhole camera]{.tag} A point with coordinates $(X, Y, Z)$ in the camera frame, $Z > 0$, is imaged at $(f X / Z,\ f Y / Z)$ in the focal plane, where $f$ is the focal length.

In pixel units and homogeneous coordinates, a world point $P_w$ is imaged at $x$ with
$$
\lambda \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = K\, [R \mid t] \begin{pmatrix} P_w \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad K = \begin{pmatrix} f_p & 0 & c_x \\ 0 & f_p & c_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} .
$$

Here $(R, t)$ is the pose of the camera, $f_p$ the focal length measured in pixels, $(c_x, c_y)$ the principal point and $\lambda > 0$ a scale factor.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.2 — Images of a plane are related by homographies]{.tag} The images of a planar scene taken by two pinhole cameras are related by a homography: there is an invertible $3 \times 3$ matrix $H$ such that corresponding points satisfy
$$
\tilde x_2 \sim H\, \tilde x_1 ,
$$
where $\tilde x$ denotes homogeneous coordinates and $\sim$ equality up to a non-zero factor. The same holds for any scene when the camera only rotates about its centre, with $H = K R K^{-1}$.

::: proof
Choose world coordinates in which the plane is $Z_w = 0$. A point $(X, Y, 0)$ is imaged by the first camera at
$$
\tilde x_1 \sim K_1 [r_1\ r_2\ t] \begin{pmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = H_1 \begin{pmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 1 \end{pmatrix},
$$
where $r_1, r_2$ are the first two columns of $R$. When the camera centre is not on the plane, $H_1$ is invertible, and likewise $H_2$ for the second camera. Hence $\tilde x_2 \sim H_2 H_1^{-1} \tilde x_1$.

For a pure rotation, $\tilde x_1 \sim K P$ and $\tilde x_2 \sim K R P$ for the same point $P$ of the camera frame, so $\tilde x_2 \sim K R K^{-1} \tilde x_1$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Homographies, and their affine approximations for small fields of view, are the geometric transforms that an image-processing chain must apply to pixels. Lens distortion adds a radial term, often modelled as $x_d = x (1 + k_1 r^2 + k_2 r^4)$, which is estimated by calibration and then undone by resampling — again an interpolation problem ([ch. 2–3](#ch2)).

::: ex
[Example 1.3 — How small are real displacements?]{.tag} A camera with $f_p = 3000$ pixels observes a scene at depth $Z = 10$ m and moves sideways by $b = 1$ mm between two shots. A point of the scene moves in the image by
$$
f_p\, \frac{b}{Z} = 3000 \times \frac{0.001}{10} = 0.3 \ \text{pixel}.
$$

Measuring such a displacement is a *sub-pixel* problem. Ch. 6 shows that it can be solved to a few hundredths of a pixel when the images are well sampled.
:::

### 1.2 Diffraction and the optical cut-off frequency

Light is a wave. A lens with a finite aperture cannot focus a point of the scene into a point of the sensor; it produces a small diffraction pattern instead. The remarkable consequence is that optical images are band-limited.

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.4 — Incoherent diffraction-limited imaging is band-limited]{.tag} Consider an aberration-free optical system with a circular pupil of diameter $D$ and focal distance $f$, of f-number $N = f / D$. Assume monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda$, incoherent illumination and the Fraunhofer approximation.

The irradiance on the sensor is $E = O * h$, where $O$ is the geometric image and $h$ is the **Airy pattern**
$$
h(r) = C \Big( \frac{2 J_1(v)}{v} \Big)^2, \qquad v = \frac{\pi r}{\lambda N},
$$
with $J_1$ the Bessel function of order 1 and $C$ a normalising constant.

Its Fourier transform, the optical transfer function, vanishes above the cut-off frequency:
$$
\nu_c = \frac{1}{\lambda N} \ \text{cycles per unit length}.
$$

For $s = \nu / \nu_c \in [0, 1]$, it equals
$$
H(\nu) = \frac{2}{\pi} \Big( \arccos s - s \sqrt{1 - s^2} \Big).
$$

::: proof
We give the precise sketch; the details are in chapter 6 of Goodman's *Introduction to Fourier Optics* (3rd edition).

1.  In the Fraunhofer approximation, the complex amplitude produced in the focal plane by a point source is the Fourier transform of the pupil function $P$ (the indicator of a disc of radius $D/2$), evaluated at the scaled frequency $2\pi x / (\lambda f)$.
2.  With incoherent light, the intensities of different points add, not their amplitudes. The irradiance point-spread function is therefore $h = |a|^2$, where $a$ is the amplitude of step 1. The 2D Fourier transform of the indicator of a disc is a multiple of $J_1(\rho)/\rho$, which gives the Airy formula.
3.  The Fourier transform of $|a|^2$ is the autocorrelation of $P$, up to the same scaling. The autocorrelation of a disc of radius $D/2$ is supported in the disc of radius $D$, which becomes the frequency $\nu_c = D / (\lambda f)$ after scaling.
4.  The autocorrelation at shift $d$ is the area of the intersection of two discs of radius $D/2$ whose centres are $d$ apart. Divided by the area of one disc, with $s = d / D$, it is the formula for $H$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The first zero of $J_1$ is at $v \approx 3.832$, so the dark ring of the Airy pattern has radius $1.22\, \lambda N$. A sensor samples the irradiance without aliasing only if its Nyquist frequency $1/(2p)$, for a pixel pitch $p$, exceeds $\nu_c$. That is, only if
$$
p \le \frac{\lambda N}{2}.
$$

::: ex
[Example 1.5 — A diffraction budget]{.tag} Take green light, $\lambda = 0.55$ µm, and an aperture $N = 2.8$.

-   The cut-off frequency is $\nu_c = 1 / (0.55 \times 10^{-3} \times 2.8) \approx 649$ cycles/mm, and the first Airy zero lies at $1.88$ µm.
-   Aliasing-free sampling would need a pitch $p \le 0.77$ µm, smaller than the pixels of nearly all current cameras (only the smallest smartphone pixels, around 0.6 µm, come close).
-   With $p = 2$ µm, the Nyquist frequency is $250$ cycles/mm and the optical transfer function there is $H = 0.522$: half of the contrast of the finest representable frequency survives the optics, and frequencies between 250 and 649 cycles/mm, which the optics let through, will alias.

The numbers are computed by Code 1.9. Real cameras are therefore not exactly Shannon-sampled; the pixel integration of the next section attenuates the aliased frequencies further.
:::

### 1.3 Pixel integration and the total point-spread function

::: def
[Definition 1.6 — Pixel integration and total PSF]{.tag} A photosite of side $c$, at most the pitch $p$, integrates the irradiance over its square. In pixel units ($p = 1$), the measured value at the grid point $k$ is $(E * \chi_c)(k)$ up to a constant factor, where
$$
\chi_c = \frac{1}{c^2} \mathbf{1}_{[-c/2,\, c/2]^2}, \qquad \hat \chi_c(\xi) = \prod_{j=1}^{2} \frac{\sin(c \xi_j / 2)}{c \xi_j / 2} .
$$

The **total point-spread function** of the camera is the convolution of all the blurs met along the way:
$$
K = h_{\text{diffraction}} * h_{\text{aberrations, defocus}} * h_{\text{motion}} * \chi_c .
$$
:::

With a fill factor of 100 % ($c = 1$), the pixel alone attenuates the Nyquist frequency $\xi = \pi$ by $\sin(\pi/2)/(\pi/2) = 2/\pi \approx 0.637$. Some cameras add a birefringent optical low-pass filter in front of the sensor to attenuate aliasing further.

Because $K$ is a convolution of several kernels, the central limit theorem suggests a Gaussian approximation $K \approx g_\sigma$, with $\sigma$ measured in pixels. Its gain at the Nyquist frequency is $e^{-\sigma^2 \pi^2 / 2}$:

| $\sigma$ (pixels) | 0.4 | 0.6 | 0.8 | 1.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| gain at $\xi = \pi$ | 0.454 | 0.169 | 0.042 | 0.007 |

An image whose PSF has $\sigma \approx 0.8$ pixel is nearly free of aliasing but slightly blurred; with $\sigma = 0.4$, it is sharp but aliased. This tension reappears as the central trade-off of [ch. 4](#ch4).

### 1.4 Sampling and aliasing

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.7 — Spectrum of a sampled image]{.tag} Let $v = K * u$ be the irradiance image, assumed to be a Schwartz function on $\mathbb{R}^2$. The discrete-time Fourier transform of its samples is the $2\pi$-periodisation of $\hat v$:
$$
\sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}^2} v(k)\, e^{-i \langle k, \xi \rangle} = \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}^2} \hat v(\xi + 2\pi m) .
$$

On the band $[-\pi, \pi]^2$, the samples therefore see $\hat v(\xi)$ plus the aliased terms $\hat v(\xi + 2\pi m)$ for $m \neq 0$.

::: proof
Apply the second form of Theorem 0.2 in each variable, or directly the $d$-dimensional Poisson formula. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 1.8 — Folding of frequencies]{.tag} In one dimension, a frequency of $\nu$ cycles per pixel is seen at $\nu - \mathrm{round}(\nu)$.

-   A cosine at $0.7$ cycle/pixel is indistinguishable from one at $0.3$, because for every integer $k$
    $$
    \cos(2\pi \times 0.7\, k) = \cos(2\pi (1 - 0.3) k) = \cos(2\pi \times 0.3\, k) .
    $$
-   In two dimensions, stripes of frequency $(0.6, 0.1)$ cycle/pixel are seen as $(-0.4, 0.1)$. Their spacing *and* their orientation change.

This is the moiré of fabrics and brick walls in photographs: false patterns with a different period and a different direction.
:::

**Code 1.9 — The acquisition budget.** The script evaluates the diffraction transfer function, the pixel attenuation and the folding of a pure frequency.

```python
import numpy as np

# 1. Diffraction-limited OTF of a circular pupil (incoherent light)
lam, N = 0.55e-3, 2.8                     # wavelength (mm), f-number
nu_c = 1 / (lam * N)                      # cut-off frequency (cycles/mm)
def otf(nu):
    s = np.clip(nu / nu_c, 0, 1)
    return 2 / np.pi * (np.arccos(s) - s * np.sqrt(1 - s**2))
print(f"cut-off {nu_c:.0f} cycles/mm, first Airy zero {1.22*lam*N*1e3:.2f} um")
for p_um in [1.0, 2.0, 4.0]:              # pixel pitch (micrometres)
    nyq = 1 / (2 * p_um * 1e-3)           # Nyquist frequency (cycles/mm)
    pix = np.sinc(nyq * p_um * 1e-3)      # 100 % fill-factor pixel: sinc(1/2)
    print(f"pitch {p_um} um: Nyquist {nyq:.0f} c/mm, OTF {otf(nyq):.3f}, "
          f"pixel {pix:.3f}, total {otf(nyq)*pix:.3f}")

# 2. Aliasing of a pure frequency: 0.7 cycles/pixel is seen as 0.3
k = np.arange(64)
x = np.cos(2 * np.pi * 0.7 * k)
print("max |cos(2pi 0.7 k) - cos(2pi 0.3 k)| =", np.max(abs(x - np.cos(2*np.pi*0.3*k))))

# 3. Gaussian PSF: gain at Nyquist (xi = pi) as a function of sigma (pixels)
for sigma in [0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0]:
    print(f"sigma = {sigma}: ghat(pi) = {np.exp(-sigma**2*np.pi**2/2):.3f}")
```

For pitches of 1, 2 and 4 µm, the product of the optical and pixel attenuations at the Nyquist frequency is 0.081, 0.332 and 0.482. Large pixels give a sharper-looking but more aliased image; small pixels approach Shannon sampling at the cost of contrast and of light per pixel.

### 1.5 Noise and quantisation

::: def
[Definition 1.10 — Noise model]{.tag} The value recorded at pixel $k$ is
$$
u_d(k) = v(k) + n(k),
$$
where the noise terms $n(k)$ are independent, centred, and have the signal-dependent variance
$$
\mathrm{Var}\, n(k) = a\, v(k) + b .
$$

The term $a\, v(k)$ comes from photon noise: the number of photo-electrons is a Poisson variable, whose variance equals its mean. The constant $b$ collects read-out and thermal noise.
:::

Quantisation with step $\Delta$ adds an error that is close to uniform on $[-\Delta/2, \Delta/2]$ when the signal varies over many steps. Its variance is
$$
\frac{1}{\Delta} \int_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2} t^2\, dt = \frac{\Delta^2}{12} .
$$

Noise sets the ultimate precision of every sub-pixel measurement: [ch. 6.2](#ch6) turns this into a lower bound, and [ch. 7.3](#ch7) shows how noise lowers the phase coherence of an image.

### 1.6 The acquisition model

::: def
[Definition 1.11 — Acquisition model and well-sampled images]{.tag} A digital image of size $M \times N$ is modelled as
$$
u_d = \Pi_\Omega (K * u) + n ,
$$
where $u$ is the ideal continuous image, $K$ the total PSF, $\Pi_\Omega$ the restriction to the grid $\Omega = \{0, \dots, M-1\} \times \{0, \dots, N-1\}$, and $n$ the noise.

The acquisition is **well sampled** when $\widehat{K * u}$ is negligible outside $[-\pi, \pi]^2$. The samples then determine $K * u$ ([ch. 2](#ch2)), and every geometric operation on the image can be computed on this continuous model.
:::

The rest of the course follows this model. Interpolation ([ch. 2–3](#ch2)) reconstructs $K * u$ from well-sampled data. Reduction ([ch. 4](#ch4)) produces well-sampled images from finer ones. Derivatives ([ch. 5](#ch5)), sub-pixel geometry ([ch. 6](#ch6)) and the phase analysis ([ch. 7](#ch7)) are all computed on the reconstructed continuous image.

::: recap
[Key takeaways — chapter 1]{.tag}

-   The pinhole model maps planes to planes by homographies; real displacements between views are often fractions of a pixel.
-   Diffraction makes optical images band-limited, with cut-off $1/(\lambda N)$ cycles per unit length.
-   Pixel integration multiplies the spectrum by a product of cardinal sines; the total PSF is a convolution of several blurs.
-   Sampling periodises the spectrum: frequencies beyond the Nyquist limit fold back and change both period and orientation.
-   Noise is signal-dependent (photon noise) plus constant (read-out); quantisation adds $\Delta^2/12$.
-   An image is well sampled when its spectrum is negligible outside $[-\pi, \pi]^2$; most of the course relies on this property.
:::

## 2. Shannon sampling and Fourier interpolation {#ch2}

When can the samples of an image determine the continuous image, and how do we compute it between the pixels? This chapter answers the question for infinite signals (the Shannon–Whittaker theorem), then for the finite images we actually store, where the DFT gives exact sub-pixel translations and zooms. The last section removes the artefacts created by the borders of a finite image.

### 2.1 The Shannon–Whittaker theorem

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.1 — Shannon–Whittaker sampling theorem]{.tag} Let $u \in L^2(\mathbb{R})$ be band-limited, that is, $\hat u(\xi) = 0$ for $|\xi| > \pi$. Then $u$ is continuous and
$$
u(x) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} u(k)\, \mathrm{sinc}(x - k), \qquad \mathrm{sinc}(t) = \frac{\sin \pi t}{\pi t},
$$
where the series converges in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ and uniformly on $\mathbb{R}$.

::: proof
Since $\hat u \in L^2([-\pi, \pi]) \subset L^1([-\pi, \pi])$, the inversion formula holds and shows that $u$ is continuous.

Expand $\hat u$ in Fourier series on $[-\pi, \pi]$, in $L^2$:
$$
\hat u(\xi) = \sum_{k} c_k\, e^{-i k \xi}, \qquad c_k = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \hat u(\xi)\, e^{i k \xi}\, d\xi = u(k) ,
$$
the last equality being the inversion formula at $x = k$.

Apply the inversion formula to the partial sums. A direct computation gives
$$
\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} e^{-i k \xi}\, e^{i x \xi}\, d\xi = \mathrm{sinc}(x - k) .
$$

Let $S_N$ be the partial sum of the Fourier series for $|k| \le N$. By Plancherel, the $L^2$ error of the truncated sinc series equals $\|\hat u - S_N\|_{L^2} / \sqrt{2\pi}$, which tends to 0.

By Cauchy–Schwarz on $[-\pi, \pi]$, the uniform error is at most $\|\hat u - S_N\|_{L^2} / \sqrt{2\pi}$ as well, hence uniform convergence. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key result — Shannon–Whittaker interpolation]{.tag}
$$
\operatorname{supp} \hat u \subset [-\pi, \pi] \ \Longrightarrow\ u(x) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} u(k)\, \mathrm{sinc}(x - k)
$$
:::

The theorem extends to two dimensions with the tensor kernel $\mathrm{sinc}(x)\, \mathrm{sinc}(y)$ and the band $[-\pi, \pi]^2$. The band is sharp: the function $\sin(\pi x)$ has frequency exactly $\pi$ and vanishes at every integer, so the samples cannot distinguish it from zero.

The theorem has two practical weaknesses. The kernel decays only like $1/|x|$, so a truncated series converges slowly. And real images are finite and not exactly band-limited. Sections 2.2 and 2.3 address both.

### 2.2 What happens without band-limitation

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — Aliasing error bound]{.tag} Let $u$ be a Schwartz function on $\mathbb{R}$, and let $\tilde u$ be the band-limited function obtained by Shannon interpolation of its samples. Then
$$
\hat{\tilde u}(\xi) = \mathbf{1}_{[-\pi, \pi]}(\xi) \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} \hat u(\xi + 2\pi m) ,
$$

and the interpolation error is bounded by the spectral mass outside the band:
$$
\sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} |u(x) - \tilde u(x)| \le \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{|\xi| > \pi} |\hat u(\xi)|\, d\xi .
$$

::: proof
The samples of $\tilde u$ and $u$ coincide, so their discrete-time Fourier transforms coincide. By Theorem 0.2 the latter is the periodisation of $\hat u$, and the transform of $\tilde u$ is its restriction to $[-\pi, \pi]$.

The transform of the error $u - \tilde u$ is $\hat u$ outside the band, minus the aliased copies $\hat u(\xi + 2\pi m)$, $m \neq 0$, inside it.

The $L^1$ norm of the first part is $\int_{|\xi| > \pi} |\hat u|$. That of the second part is at most the same quantity, because the copies, translated back, tile the outside of the band. The inversion formula bounds the sup norm by $1/(2\pi)$ times the sum of the two $L^1$ norms. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The error has two halves of equal size: the high frequencies that are lost, and the same high frequencies that come back, folded, as false low frequencies.

::: ex
[Example 2.3 — A Gaussian spot]{.tag} Sample the Gaussian density $g_\sigma$ and interpolate it with Shannon's formula.

-   For $\sigma = 0.6$ pixel, the bound of Proposition 2.2 is 11.9 % of the peak value $g_\sigma(0)$, and the actual worst error, computed numerically, is 6.4 %.
-   For $\sigma = 1$ pixel, the bound drops to 0.34 % and the actual error to 0.17 %.
-   If the spot is centred halfway between two samples instead of on a sample, the worst error reaches the bound (11.9 % and 0.34 %): the folded copies then add up in phase with the lost frequencies, and the inequality of Proposition 2.2 is essentially sharp.

The ratio between the two values of $\sigma$ reflects the Gaussian decay of $\hat g_\sigma$ beyond $\pi$. Relative to the peak, the bound equals
$$
2\, \mathrm{erfc}\big( \sigma \pi / \sqrt 2 \big) .
$$

The script below reproduces the four numbers.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.special import erfc

k = np.arange(-60, 61)                          # enough samples: g decays fast
x = np.linspace(-8, 8, 16001)                   # fine evaluation grid
S = np.sinc(x[:, None] - k[None, :])            # Shannon kernel sinc(x - k)
for s in [0.6, 1.0]:
    bound = 2 * erfc(s * np.pi / np.sqrt(2))    # Proposition 2.2, relative to g(0)
    for c in [0.0, 0.5]:                        # spot on a sample, or halfway
        g = lambda t: np.exp(-(t - c)**2 / (2 * s**2)) / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi * s**2)
        err = np.max(np.abs(g(x) - S @ g(k))) * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi * s**2)
        print(f"sigma = {s}, centre {c}: error {100 * err:.2f} %, bound {100 * bound:.2f} %")
```
:::

### 2.3 Discrete Shannon interpolation of a finite image

A stored image has finitely many pixels. The natural continuous model is a trigonometric polynomial whose DFT coefficients are those of the image.

::: def
[Definition 2.4 — Discrete Shannon interpolate]{.tag} Let $u \in \mathbb{R}^M$, with DFT $\hat u$ and signed frequencies $p$. If $M$ is odd, its Shannon interpolate is
$$
U(x) = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{|p| \le (M-1)/2} \hat u_p\, e^{2 i \pi p x / M} .
$$

If $M$ is even, the Nyquist coefficient is split equally between the frequencies $\pm M/2$:
$$
U(x) = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{|p| < M/2} \hat u_p\, e^{2 i \pi p x / M} + \frac{1}{M}\, \hat u_{M/2} \cos(\pi x) .
$$

For an image of size $M \times N$, the interpolate is the tensor product of the two one-dimensional rules.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.5 — Properties of the discrete Shannon interpolate]{.tag} The function $U$ of Definition 2.4 is real, $M$-periodic, and interpolates: $U(k) = u_k$ for every integer $k$. It can be written with a periodic sinc kernel,
$$
U(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{M-1} u_k\, s_M(x - k),
$$
where the kernel depends on the parity of $M$:
$$
s_M(x) = \frac{\sin \pi x}{M \sin(\pi x / M)} \ (M \text{ odd}), \qquad s_M(x) = \frac{\sin \pi x}{M \tan(\pi x / M)} \ (M \text{ even}).
$$

Moreover, $U$ is the Shannon interpolate of the $M$-periodised samples, in the sense of symmetric partial sums:
$$
U(x) = \lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{|n| \le N} u_{n \bmod M}\, \mathrm{sinc}(x - n) .
$$

::: proof
*Real and interpolating.* The coefficients of $p$ and $-p$ are conjugate (Proposition 0.4), so their terms add up to a real number. At an integer $k$, $\cos(\pi k) = e^{i \pi k}$, and $U(k)$ is exactly the inverse DFT.

*Kernel, odd $M$.* Substitute the definition of $\hat u_p$ in $U$. Summing the geometric series in $p$ gives the Dirichlet kernel, with $t = 2\pi x / M$:
$$
\frac{1}{M} \sum_{|p| \le (M-1)/2} e^{i p t} = \frac{\sin(M t / 2)}{M \sin(t / 2)} = \frac{\sin \pi x}{M \sin(\pi x / M)} .
$$

*Kernel, even $M$.* The sum over $|p| \le M/2 - 1$ equals $\sin((M-1)t/2) / \sin(t/2)$. Adding $\cos(Mt/2)$ and using the identity
$$
\sin\big((M-1)t/2\big) = \sin(Mt/2)\cos(t/2) - \cos(Mt/2)\sin(t/2)
$$

gives $\sin(Mt/2)\cot(t/2)$, which is the formula.

*Periodised sinc.* Group the terms $n = k + jM$. The classical partial-fraction expansions of $\pi / \sin(\pi y)$ (for odd $M$, alternating signs) and $\pi \cot(\pi y)$ (for even $M$), summed symmetrically, give $\sum_j \mathrm{sinc}(x - k - jM) = s_M(x - k)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The even case is not a detail. Images from cameras have even sizes, and the choice of the cosine for the Nyquist term is the only one that makes $U$ real, interpolating and symmetric. It has a price, shown in Proposition 2.6.

### 2.4 Exact translation and zoom with the FFT

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.6 — Fourier translation and zoom]{.tag} Let $u \in \mathbb{R}^M$ with Shannon interpolate $U$.

1.  For odd $M$, define $T_\tau u$ by multiplying the DFT by a phase ramp:
    $$
    \widehat{T_\tau u}_p = e^{-2 i \pi p \tau / M}\, \hat u_p .
    $$
    Then $(T_\tau u)_k = U(k - \tau)$. The operator $T_\tau$ is unitary, and $T_\tau T_\sigma = T_{\tau + \sigma}$.
2.  For even $M$, the same formula holds for $|p| < M/2$, while the Nyquist coefficient is multiplied by $\cos(\pi \tau)$. In particular $T_{1/2}$ cancels it and is not invertible.
3.  For odd $M$ and an integer $z \ge 1$, the zoomed signal $(U(j/z))_{0 \le j < zM}$ is $z$ times the inverse DFT, of size $zM$, of the spectrum of $u$ padded with zeros.

::: proof
1.  The trigonometric polynomial $x \mapsto U(x - \tau)$ has coefficients $e^{-2 i \pi p \tau / M} \hat u_p$; sampling it at the integers gives the claim. The multipliers have modulus 1, so $T_\tau$ preserves the energy by Parseval, and phase ramps compose additively.
2.  The Nyquist term of $U(k - \tau)$ is proportional to $\cos(\pi(k - \tau)) = (-1)^k \cos(\pi \tau)$, because $\sin(\pi k) = 0$.
3.  The inverse DFT of size $zM$ of the padded spectrum, multiplied by $z$, equals $\frac{1}{M} \sum_p \hat u_p e^{2 i \pi p (j/z) / M} = U(j/z)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The translation of item 1 is the reference sub-pixel translation of the course. It is exact for the band-limited periodic model, it can be undone, and translations compose without accumulating any blur. Item 2 is the reason why the code below works with odd sizes, or treats the Nyquist coefficient explicitly.

**Code 2.7 — Shannon interpolation, translation and zoom.** The script evaluates $U$ at arbitrary points, translates by FFT, checks invertibility for odd and even sizes, and zooms by zero-padding.

```python
import numpy as np

def shannon_eval(u, x):
    """Evaluate the real trigonometric (Shannon) interpolate of u at the points x."""
    M = len(u)
    U = np.fft.fft(u)
    p = np.fft.fftfreq(M, d=1 / M)                 # signed integer frequencies
    w = np.ones(M)
    if M % 2 == 0:                                 # split the Nyquist coefficient
        p, U, w = np.append(p, M // 2), np.append(U, U[M // 2]), np.append(w, 0.5)
        w[M // 2] = 0.5
    E = np.exp(2j * np.pi * np.outer(x, p) / M)
    return (E @ (w * U)).real / M

def shannon_shift(u, tau):
    """Exact sub-pixel translation k -> U(k - tau) (Proposition 2.6)."""
    M = len(u)
    p = np.fft.fftfreq(M, d=1 / M)
    phase = np.exp(-2j * np.pi * p * tau / M)
    if M % 2 == 0:
        phase[M // 2] = np.cos(np.pi * tau)        # Nyquist coefficient
    return np.fft.ifft(np.fft.fft(u) * phase).real

def fourier_zoom(u, z):
    """Zoom by an integer factor z (M odd): zero-padding of the centred spectrum."""
    M = len(u)
    pad = np.zeros(z * M, complex)
    c = z * M // 2 - M // 2
    pad[c:c + M] = np.fft.fftshift(np.fft.fft(u))
    return np.fft.ifft(np.fft.ifftshift(pad)).real * z

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
for M in (9, 8):
    u = rng.normal(size=M)
    print(f"M = {M}: interpolates {np.allclose(shannon_eval(u, np.arange(M)), u)}, "
          f"shift = evaluation {np.allclose(shannon_shift(u, 0.3), shannon_eval(u, np.arange(M) - 0.3))}")
    back = shannon_shift(shannon_shift(shannon_shift(u, 0.5), 0.5), -1.0)
    print(f"        error after +1/2, +1/2, -1: {np.max(abs(back - u)):.2e}")
u = rng.normal(size=9)
print("zero-padding zoom = Shannon evaluation:",
      np.allclose(fourier_zoom(u, 4), shannon_eval(u, np.arange(36) / 4)))
```

For $M = 9$, two half-pixel translations followed by a translation of $-1$ return the signal to $4 \times 10^{-16}$. For $M = 8$, the error is $0.30$: the first half-pixel translation destroyed the Nyquist coefficient. Exercise 7 asks for a proof and a fix.

### 2.5 Borders: the periodic plus smooth decomposition

The DFT treats an image as periodic. Its left and right borders, top and bottom borders, are glued together, and the jump between them acts like a sharp edge. In the spectrum this jump creates a bright cross along the frequency axes. In interpolation it creates ringing along the borders, and in translation it makes content wrap around.

The decomposition of Moisan (2011), one of the official references of the course, splits the image into a periodic component, which carries the content and has a clean spectrum, and a smooth component, which absorbs the border jumps.

::: def
[Definition 2.8 — Boundary image]{.tag} For an image $u$ on $\Omega = \{0, \dots, M-1\} \times \{0, \dots, N-1\}$, the boundary image is $v = v_1 + v_2$, where
$$
v_1(x, y) = \begin{cases} u(M-1-x,\, y) - u(x, y) & \text{if } x \in \{0, M-1\}, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}, \end{cases}
$$

and $v_2$ is defined in the same way along the second coordinate. At each border pixel, $v$ is the jump towards the opposite border, the pixel that becomes its neighbour when the image is made periodic.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.9 — Periodic plus smooth decomposition (Moisan, 2011)]{.tag} Let $I$ be the set of pairs of 4-neighbours inside $\Omega$, and $B$ the set of pairs of pixels that become neighbours only through periodisation (opposite border pixels). Among all decompositions $u = p + s$, consider the energy
$$
E(p, s) = \sum_{\{a, b\} \in B} \big(p(a) - p(b)\big)^2 + \sum_{\{a, b\} \in I} \big(s(a) - s(b)\big)^2 .
$$

There is a unique minimiser with $s$ of zero mean. Its smooth component is the zero-mean solution of $\Delta_{\mathrm{per}}\, s = v$, where $\Delta_{\mathrm{per}}$ is the 5-point Laplacian with periodic boundary conditions. In Fourier, for $(q, r) \neq (0, 0)$,
$$
\hat s(q, r) = \frac{\hat v(q, r)}{2 \cos(2\pi q / M) + 2 \cos(2\pi r / N) - 4}, \qquad \hat s(0, 0) = 0 .
$$

In particular, $s$ is discrete-harmonic at every interior pixel, and $p = u - s$ is computed with two FFTs.

::: proof
Substitute $p = u - s$. The energy becomes a quadratic function of $s$ alone. Its derivative with respect to $s(a)$ vanishes when
$$
\sum_{b \sim_I a} \big(s(a) - s(b)\big) + \sum_{b \sim_B a} \big(s(a) - s(b)\big) = \sum_{b \sim_B a} \big(u(a) - u(b)\big) .
$$

The left-hand side runs over the four periodic neighbours of $a$, so it equals $-\Delta_{\mathrm{per}} s(a)$. The right-hand side is $-v(a)$ by Definition 2.8. The optimality condition is thus $\Delta_{\mathrm{per}} s = v$.

The DFT diagonalises $\Delta_{\mathrm{per}}$, with the eigenvalues in the denominator above. They are negative except at $(0,0)$. The image $v$ has zero mean, since each pair of $B$ contributes two opposite values; so the equation has a solution, unique up to a constant.

The quadratic part of the energy, $\sum_I (s(a) - s(b))^2$ plus a sum of squares, vanishes only for constant $s$ because $\Omega$ is connected. The energy is therefore strictly convex on zero-mean images, and the critical point is the unique minimiser.

Finally, $v = 0$ at interior pixels, where $\Delta_{\mathrm{per}}$ is the ordinary Laplacian; hence $\Delta s = 0$ there. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

**Code 2.10 — Periodic plus smooth decomposition.** The image below is deliberately non-periodic: a ramp, an oblique texture and a disc.

```python
import numpy as np

def per_smooth(u):
    """Periodic plus smooth decomposition u = p + s (Moisan, 2011)."""
    M, N = u.shape
    v = np.zeros_like(u)
    v[0, :] += u[-1, :] - u[0, :]            # jumps across the periodic boundary
    v[-1, :] += u[0, :] - u[-1, :]
    v[:, 0] += u[:, -1] - u[:, 0]
    v[:, -1] += u[:, 0] - u[:, -1]
    q = np.arange(M)[:, None]
    r = np.arange(N)[None, :]
    den = 2 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * q / M) + 2 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * r / N) - 4
    den[0, 0] = 1.0                          # avoid 0/0; the mean of s is set to 0
    s_hat = np.fft.fft2(v) / den
    s_hat[0, 0] = 0.0
    s = np.fft.ifft2(s_hat).real
    return u - s, s

M = N = 128
y, x = np.mgrid[0:M, 0:N].astype(float)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
u = 0.8 * x + 0.5 * y + 20 * np.sin(0.9 * x + 0.4 * y) + 60 * ((x - 70)**2 + (y - 50)**2 < 300)
u += rng.normal(0, 2, u.shape)
p, s = per_smooth(u)

def axis_energy(img):
    """Fraction of non-DC spectral energy lying on the two frequency axes."""
    E = np.abs(np.fft.fft2(img - img.mean()))**2
    return (E[0, 1:].sum() + E[1:, 0].sum()) / E.sum()

print(f"energy on the axes: u {axis_energy(u):.3f}   p {axis_energy(p):.3f}")
lap = np.roll(s, 1, 0) + np.roll(s, -1, 0) + np.roll(s, 1, 1) + np.roll(s, -1, 1) - 4 * s
print(f"max |Laplacian(s)| inside the image: {np.abs(lap[1:-1, 1:-1]).max():.1e}")
print(f"boundary jump of u: {np.abs(u[0] - u[-1]).mean():.1f}, of p: {np.abs(p[0] - p[-1]).mean():.1f}")
```

The share of spectral energy on the two axes falls from 0.797 for $u$ to 0.180 for $p$: the cross has disappeared. The mean jump across the top and bottom borders falls from 63.4 to 3.0 grey levels. The Laplacian of $s$ vanishes inside the image to $10^{-13}$, as Theorem 2.9 predicts.

In practice, FFT-based operations are applied to $p$, while $s$ — smooth and harmonic — is handled by any simple method, or added back unchanged when the operation is a filtering with small support. Two alternatives are common: mirror symmetrisation, which doubles each dimension of the image and keeps continuity but not the derivative, and apodisation by a window, which alters the content near the borders.

::: recap
[Key takeaways — chapter 2]{.tag}

-   A band-limited function is the sinc series of its samples (Theorem 2.1); without band-limitation, the error is bounded by the spectral mass beyond $\pi$, half lost and half folded back.
-   A finite image is interpolated by the trigonometric polynomial with the same DFT; for even sizes the Nyquist coefficient becomes a cosine.
-   Sub-pixel translation is a phase ramp on the DFT: exact, unitary and composable for odd sizes; for even sizes, the half-pixel translation kills the Nyquist coefficient.
-   Zooming is zero-padding of the spectrum.
-   The periodic plus smooth decomposition removes the border jump; its smooth part solves a Poisson equation, in two FFTs.
:::

## 3. Splines and lossless geometric transforms {#ch3}

Shannon interpolation is exact for band-limited periodic images but global: every output value depends on every pixel. Local kernels are cheaper and handle non-periodic images, but they blur. This chapter compares interpolation kernels through their frequency responses, builds the B-spline family, and then asks which geometric transforms can be applied to an image without any loss.

### 3.1 Interpolation kernels

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Interpolation kernel]{.tag} Let $\varphi$ be a continuous integrable function. The *direct* interpolation of a sequence $u$ is
$$
U(x) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} u_k\, \varphi(x - k) .
$$

It interpolates, $U(k) = u_k$, exactly when $\varphi(0) = 1$ and $\varphi(k) = 0$ for every integer $k \neq 0$.

A *generalised* interpolation uses coefficients $c = (c_k)$ computed from $u$ by a discrete prefilter, so that $U = \sum_k c_k \varphi(\cdot - k)$ interpolates even when $\varphi$ does not. In 2D, the kernel is the tensor product $\varphi(x)\varphi(y)$.
:::

The classical kernels are nearest neighbour ($\beta^0$, the box), linear interpolation ($\beta^1$, the hat), the cubic convolution kernel of Keys (1981), cubic splines, and the sinc of [ch. 2](#ch2). With the parameter $a = -1/2$, the Keys kernel is
$$
\varphi_{\mathrm{K}}(x) = \begin{cases} \tfrac32 |x|^3 - \tfrac52 |x|^2 + 1 & |x| \le 1, \\ -\tfrac12 |x|^3 + \tfrac52 |x|^2 - 4|x| + 2 & 1 < |x| < 2, \\ 0 & |x| \ge 2 . \end{cases}
$$

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — Reproduction of constants]{.tag} Let $\varphi$ be continuous with compact support. Then the shifted kernels form a partition of unity,
$$
\sum_{k} \varphi(x - k) = 1 \quad \text{for all } x ,
$$
if and only if $\hat \varphi(0) = 1$ and $\hat \varphi(2\pi m) = 0$ for every integer $m \neq 0$.

::: proof
The function $F(x) = \sum_k \varphi(x - k)$ is 1-periodic and continuous. As in the proof of Theorem 0.2, its Fourier coefficients are $c_m(F) = \hat \varphi(2\pi m)$. A continuous periodic function equals the constant 1 if and only if its Fourier coefficients are $c_0 = 1$ and $c_m = 0$ otherwise. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Reproducing constants is the minimum one asks of an interpolator: a flat image must stay flat. More generally, when $\hat \varphi(0) \neq 0$ and $\hat \varphi$ has zeros of order $L$ at every $2\pi m$, $m \neq 0$, the integer shifts of the kernel span the polynomials of degree less than $L$.

A smooth image sampled with step $h$ is then approximated with an error of order $h^L$. These are the Strang–Fix conditions, reviewed by Thévenaz, Blu and Unser (2000).

| Kernel | Support | Approximation order $L$ |
|---|---|---|
| nearest neighbour $\beta^0$ | 1 | 1 |
| linear $\beta^1$ | 2 | 2 |
| Keys, $a = -1/2$ | 4 | 3 |
| cubic spline interpolation | infinite, exponential decay | 4 |
| Shannon (sinc) | infinite, decay in $1/\lvert x\rvert$ | exact on band-limited signals |

### 3.2 B-splines

::: def
[Definition 3.3 — B-splines]{.tag} The centred B-spline of degree $n$ is defined recursively by
$$
\beta^0 = \mathbf{1}_{[-1/2,\, 1/2)}, \qquad \beta^n = \beta^0 * \beta^{n-1} .
$$

By the convolution rule, its Fourier transform is
$$
\hat \beta^n(\xi) = \Big( \frac{\sin(\xi / 2)}{\xi / 2} \Big)^{n+1} .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.4 — Properties of B-splines]{.tag}

1.  $\beta^n$ is non-negative, has integral 1 and support $[-(n+1)/2,\ (n+1)/2]$.
2.  $\beta^n$ is a piecewise polynomial of degree $n$, of class $C^{n-1}$.
3.  The integer shifts of $\beta^n$ form a partition of unity, and $\beta^n$ has approximation order $n + 1$.
4.  The cubic B-spline is
    $$
    \beta^3(x) = \begin{cases} \tfrac23 - |x|^2 + \tfrac12 |x|^3 & |x| \le 1, \\ \tfrac16 (2 - |x|)^3 & 1 \le |x| < 2, \\ 0 & |x| \ge 2, \end{cases}
    $$
    with $\beta^3(0) = 2/3$ and $\beta^3(\pm 1) = 1/6$.

::: proof
1.  Positivity, mass and support are preserved by convolution with $\beta^0$, adding $1/2$ to the half-width at each step.
2.  For any integrable $f$, $(\beta^0 * f)(x) = \int_{x - 1/2}^{x + 1/2} f$, whose derivative is $f(x + 1/2) - f(x - 1/2)$. Each convolution therefore raises the degree and the smoothness by one, starting from the piecewise constant $\beta^0$.
3.  $\hat \beta^n(0) = 1$, and $\sin(\pi m) = 0$ makes $\hat \beta^n$ vanish to order $n+1$ at every $2\pi m$, $m \neq 0$. Proposition 3.2 and the Strang–Fix conditions conclude.
4.  Convolve $\beta^2$ with $\beta^0$, or check that the formula is $C^2$, has integral 1 and the right support. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 3.3 Spline interpolation by prefiltering

The cubic B-spline does not interpolate, since $\beta^3(\pm 1) \neq 0$. Spline interpolation looks for coefficients $c$ such that the spline $U = \sum_k c_k \beta^3(\cdot - k)$ passes through the samples.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.5 — Cubic spline interpolation as a recursive filter]{.tag} The interpolation conditions read $b * c = u$, where $b = (\tfrac16, \tfrac23, \tfrac16)$ is the sampled B-spline. Its symbol satisfies
$$
B(\xi) = \frac23 + \frac13 \cos \xi \ \ge\ \frac13 ,
$$
so $b$ has a stable inverse. With $z_1 = \sqrt 3 - 2 \approx -0.268$, the inverse filter is
$$
(b^{-1})_k = \sqrt 3\, z_1^{|k|} .
$$

It is computed by two first-order recursions, one causal and one anti-causal:
$$
c^+_k = u_k + z_1\, c^+_{k-1}, \qquad c^-_k = z_1 \big( c^-_{k+1} - c^+_k \big), \qquad c_k = 6\, c^-_k .
$$

::: proof
In the $z$-transform, $B(z) = (z + 4 + z^{-1}) / 6$. The number $z_1$ is a root of $z^2 + 4z + 1$, so that $-1/z_1 - z_1 = 4$, and
$$
z + 4 + z^{-1} = -\frac{1}{z_1} (1 - z_1 z^{-1})(1 - z_1 z) .
$$

Hence the inverse is a product of a causal and an anti-causal first-order filter:
$$
\frac{6}{z + 4 + z^{-1}} = 6 \cdot \frac{1}{1 - z_1 z^{-1}} \cdot \frac{-z_1}{1 - z_1 z} .
$$

Both are stable because $|z_1| < 1$. The first gives the recursion for $c^+$; the second, written as $c^-_k - z_1 c^-_{k+1} = -z_1 c^+_k$, gives the recursion for $c^-$. Expanding the two geometric series gives the impulse response $\sqrt 3\, z_1^{|k|}$, as Exercise 4 checks. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The recursions cost a few operations per sample, independently of the size, and are applied along each axis of an image. They need an initial value at each end: Unser, Aldroubi and Eden (1993) derive it for mirror boundary conditions, and with periodic conditions the filter is a simple division by $B$ in the DFT domain.

The equivalent interpolating kernel is the *cardinal cubic spline*
$$
\eta^3(x) = \sum_k (b^{-1})_k\, \beta^3(x - k), \qquad \hat \eta^3(\xi) = \frac{\hat \beta^3(\xi)}{B(\xi)} .
$$

It has infinite support but decays like $0.268^{|x|}$. As the degree tends to infinity, the cardinal splines converge to the sinc kernel (Aldroubi, Unser and Eden, 1992): splines interpolate between local kernels and Shannon interpolation.

**Code 3.7 — Spline interpolation, checked against SciPy.** The prefilter is applied in Fourier with periodic boundary conditions; the result coincides with `scipy.ndimage.shift` in mode `grid-wrap`.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import ndimage

def bspline3(x):
    x = np.abs(x)
    return np.where(x <= 1, 2/3 - x**2 + x**3 / 2, np.where(x < 2, (2 - x)**3 / 6, 0.0))

def spline_coefficients(u):
    """Periodic cubic-spline prefilter: solve b * c = u by division in Fourier."""
    M = len(u)
    B = 2/3 + (1/3) * np.cos(2 * np.pi * np.arange(M) / M)   # DFT of (1/6, 2/3, 1/6)
    return np.fft.ifft(np.fft.fft(u) / B).real

def spline_shift(u, tau):
    """Evaluate the periodic cubic-spline interpolate at the points k - tau, |tau| < 1."""
    c, M = spline_coefficients(u), len(u)
    k = np.arange(M)
    return sum(c[(k - j) % M] * bspline3(j - tau) for j in range(-2, 3))

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
u = rng.normal(size=32)
print("interpolates:", np.allclose(spline_shift(u, 0.0), u))
print("matches scipy.ndimage.shift(order=3, mode='grid-wrap'):",
      np.allclose(spline_shift(u, 0.3), ndimage.shift(u, 0.3, order=3, mode="grid-wrap")))
delta = np.zeros(32); delta[0] = 1.0
z1 = np.sqrt(3) - 2
print("impulse response = sqrt(3) z1^|k|:",
      np.allclose(spline_coefficients(delta)[:5], np.sqrt(3) * z1**np.arange(5)))
```

### 3.4 Comparing interpolators in the frequency domain

Translating samples by $\tau$ with a kernel $\varphi$ is a discrete filter. Its frequency response tells which frequencies survive. For a direct kernel, the response is
$$
H_\tau(\xi) = \sum_k \varphi(k - \tau)\, e^{-i k \xi},
$$
and for a spline it is divided by the prefilter symbol $B(\xi)$. The Shannon translation has $|H_\tau| = 1$ on the whole band. The half-pixel translation $\tau = 1/2$ is the worst case for local kernels.

**Code 3.8 — Gain of the half-pixel translation.**

```python
import numpy as np

def keys(x, a=-0.5):
    x = np.abs(x)
    return np.where(x <= 1, (a + 2) * x**3 - (a + 3) * x**2 + 1,
           np.where(x < 2, a * x**3 - 5 * a * x**2 + 8 * a * x - 4 * a, 0.0))

def bspline3(x):
    x = np.abs(x)
    return np.where(x <= 1, 2/3 - x**2 + x**3 / 2, np.where(x < 2, (2 - x)**3 / 6, 0.0))

def gain(weights_at, xi, tau=0.5, prefilter=None):
    """|frequency response| of the filter that shifts samples by tau."""
    k = np.arange(-4, 5)
    H = np.sum(weights_at(k - tau)[:, None] * np.exp(-1j * np.outer(k, xi)), axis=0)
    if prefilter is not None:
        H = H / np.sum(prefilter(k)[:, None] * np.exp(-1j * np.outer(k, xi)), axis=0)
    return np.abs(H)

xi = np.array([np.pi / 4, np.pi / 2, 3 * np.pi / 4, 0.95 * np.pi])
print("xi/pi:               ", np.round(xi / np.pi, 2))
print("linear (hat)         ", np.round(gain(lambda x: np.maximum(1 - abs(x), 0), xi), 3))
print("Keys cubic a=-1/2    ", np.round(gain(keys, xi), 3))
print("cubic B-spline interp", np.round(gain(bspline3, xi, prefilter=bspline3), 3))
print("Shannon              ", np.ones(4))
```

| Frequency $\xi$ | $\pi/4$ | $\pi/2$ | $3\pi/4$ | $0.95\pi$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| linear | 0.924 | 0.707 | 0.383 | 0.078 |
| Keys ($a = -1/2$) | 0.992 | 0.884 | 0.546 | 0.117 |
| cubic spline | 0.999 | 0.972 | 0.762 | 0.194 |
| Shannon | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |

::: ex
[Example 3.9 — The Keys gain by hand]{.tag} For $\tau = 1/2$ the Keys weights are $\varphi_{\mathrm{K}}(\pm 1/2) = 0.5625$ and $\varphi_{\mathrm{K}}(\pm 3/2) = -0.0625$. Pairing symmetric terms, the modulus of the response is
$$
|H_{1/2}(\xi)| = \big| 1.125 \cos(\xi/2) - 0.125 \cos(3\xi/2) \big| .
$$

At $\xi = \pi/2$ this gives $1.125 \times 0.7071 + 0.125 \times 0.7071 = 0.884$, the value of the table. For linear interpolation, the response is $\cos(\xi / 2)$, equal to $0.707$ at the same frequency.
:::

All local kernels attenuate the upper half of the band. One application costs little, but the attenuation compounds when transforms are chained: after ten half-pixel translations with linear interpolation, the gain at $\xi = \pi/2$ is $0.707^{10} \approx 0.031$.

### 3.5 Lossless geometric transforms

A discrete geometric transform is *lossless* when it is invertible and its inverse is a transform of the same family; ideally it is unitary, so that it preserves the energy and the noise level. A chain of lossless transforms can always be undone, and iterating them accumulates no blur.

FFT translations of odd-sized images (Proposition 2.6), integer zooms by zero-padding (which have an exact left inverse, [ch. 4.6](#ch4)), flips and rotations by multiples of 90° are lossless. Interpolation with any kernel whose gain is below 1 somewhere in the band is not. Rotations by arbitrary angles become lossless thanks to a factorisation into shears.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.10 — Rotation by three shears]{.tag} For every angle $\theta$ with $|\theta| < \pi$, with $t = \tan(\theta/2)$ and $s = \sin \theta$,
$$
\begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -t \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ s & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -t \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} .
$$

Each shear translates every row (or every column) by an amount proportional to its index. Computed with the Fourier translation of Proposition 2.6 on an image of odd width and height, each shear is a unitary operator on images. The resulting discrete rotation is therefore unitary, and its inverse is the three-shear rotation by $-\theta$.

::: proof
Multiply the first two matrices:
$$
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -t \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ s & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 - ts & -t \\ s & 1 \end{pmatrix} .
$$

Multiplying by the third gives the diagonal entries $1 - ts$ and the off-diagonal entries $s$ and $-t(1 - ts) - t = -t(2 - ts)$.

The half-angle formulas give $ts = 2 \sin^2(\theta/2) = 1 - \cos\theta$. Hence the diagonal entries equal $\cos\theta$, and the upper-right entry equals
$$
-\tan(\theta/2)\,(1 + \cos\theta) = -2 \sin(\theta/2) \cos(\theta/2) = -\sin\theta .
$$

A shear applies the unitary translation $T_{a(y - c)}$ to the row of index $y$, so it is unitary on the whole image, with inverse the shear of parameter $-a$. The inverse of the product is the product of the inverses in reverse order, which is the factorisation for $-\theta$, since $\tan$ and $\sin$ are odd. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key result — a rotation is three shears]{.tag}
$$
R_\theta = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -\tan\frac{\theta}{2} \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \sin\theta & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -\tan\frac{\theta}{2} \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
$$
:::

Three remarks keep the method honest.

-   The shears are periodic, so content pushed across a border wraps around: the image must be padded so that every intermediate image fits. For a square image of half-size $L$ and $|\theta| \le \pi/4$, following the corners shows that all three intermediate images fit in the bounding box of the rotated square, of half-size $L(|\cos\theta| + |\sin\theta|)$ (Exercise 5).
-   The discrete rotation is not *exactly* the rotation of the trigonometric polynomial of the image, because a sheared trigonometric polynomial is no longer one of the same degree. The difference is tiny for well-sampled images, as the experiment shows, and the transform is exactly invertible in any case.
-   For larger angles, one first rotates by a multiple of 90°, which is exact, so that the remaining angle satisfies $|\theta| \le \pi/4$ and $|t| \le \tan(\pi/8) \approx 0.41$.

**Code 3.11 — A full turn in 36 steps.** The test image is a sum of smooth Gaussian spots inside a zero margin, of odd size 129.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import ndimage

def shear_rows(u, a):
    """Row y is translated by a*(y - c) with the exact Fourier (Shannon) translation."""
    M, N = u.shape                                  # N odd: no Nyquist coefficient
    c = (M - 1) / 2
    p = np.fft.fftfreq(N, d=1 / N)
    tau = a * (np.arange(M) - c)
    phase = np.exp(-2j * np.pi * np.outer(tau, p) / N)
    return np.fft.ifft(np.fft.fft(u, axis=1) * phase, axis=1).real

def rotate_3shears(u, theta):
    t, s = np.tan(theta / 2), np.sin(theta)
    u = shear_rows(u, -t)
    u = shear_rows(u.T, s).T                        # vertical shear
    return shear_rows(u, -t)

n = 129
y, x = np.mgrid[0:n, 0:n] - (n - 1) / 2
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
u = np.zeros((n, n))
for _ in range(25):
    cx, cy = rng.uniform(-30, 30, 2)
    u += rng.uniform(50, 100) * np.exp(-((x - cx)**2 + (y - cy)**2) / (2 * 2.0**2))

steps, theta = 36, 2 * np.pi / 36
v_lin, v_fft = u.copy(), u.copy()
for _ in range(steps):
    v_lin = ndimage.rotate(v_lin, np.degrees(theta), reshape=False, order=1)
    v_fft = rotate_3shears(v_fft, theta)
rms = lambda e: np.sqrt(np.mean(e**2))
print(f"after a full turn in {steps} steps: RMSE bilinear {rms(v_lin - u):.2f}, "
      f"three shears {rms(v_fft - u):.2e}  (image RMS {rms(u):.2f})")
w = rotate_3shears(rotate_3shears(u, 0.7), -0.7)
print(f"rotate by 0.7 rad then back: max error {np.abs(w - u).max():.1e}")
print("energy preserved by one rotation:", np.isclose(np.sum(rotate_3shears(u, 0.7)**2), np.sum(u**2)))
```

After the full turn, bilinear interpolation leaves an RMS error of 5.12 grey levels, for an image of RMS 12.04: the spots are visibly blurred. The three-shear rotation returns the image to within $3.9 \times 10^{-8}$. A rotation by 0.7 radian followed by its inverse is exact to $10^{-13}$, and one rotation preserves the energy exactly. This is the experiment announced in the introduction.

::: recap
[Key takeaways — chapter 3]{.tag}

-   An interpolator is judged by its approximation order (zeros of $\hat \varphi$ at $2\pi m$) and by its frequency response on the band.
-   B-splines are repeated convolutions of the box; cubic spline interpolation needs a prefilter, computed by two recursions with pole $z_1 = \sqrt 3 - 2$.
-   At half a pixel, linear interpolation keeps 71 % of the amplitude at $\xi = \pi/2$, Keys 88 %, cubic splines 97 %, Shannon 100 %.
-   Losses compound when transforms are chained; lossless transforms (FFT translations, three-shear rotations) are unitary and exactly invertible.
-   $R_\theta$ is the product of three shears with parameters $-\tan(\theta/2)$, $\sin\theta$, $-\tan(\theta/2)$.
:::

## 4. Image reduction: aliasing, ringing and blur {#ch4}

Reducing an image by a factor $z$ — for a thumbnail, a pyramid, or a coarser analysis scale — means sampling it on a grid $z$ times coarser. The new grid can carry only the frequencies below $\pi / z$. Whatever we do with the frequencies above, we pay in aliasing, in ringing or in blur. This chapter measures the three defects and proves that no filter without ringing can avoid trading blur against aliasing.

### 4.1 The reduction model

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Reduction with a prefilter]{.tag} Let $U$ be the continuous model of an image ([ch. 2](#ch2)), $z > 1$ the reduction factor, and $h$ an integrable prefilter with $\int h = 1$. The reduced image is
$$
v(k) = (h * U)(z k), \qquad k \in \mathbb{Z}^d .
$$

Naive subsampling, $v(k) = u(zk)$ for an integer $z$, corresponds to $h = \delta$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — Spectrum of a reduced image]{.tag} With the notation of Definition 4.1, and $h * U$ regular enough for Theorem 0.2 to apply, the discrete-time Fourier transform of the reduced image is
$$
\sum_{k} v(k)\, e^{-i \langle k, \xi \rangle} = \frac{1}{z^d} \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}^d} \hat h\Big( \frac{\xi + 2\pi m}{z} \Big)\, \hat U\Big( \frac{\xi + 2\pi m}{z} \Big) .
$$

::: proof
The function $w(x) = (h * U)(z x)$ has Fourier transform $z^{-d} (\hat h \hat U)(\xi / z)$ by the dilation rule. Its samples are $v$, and Theorem 0.2 periodises its transform. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

On the band $[-\pi, \pi]^d$ of the coarse grid, the term $m = 0$ carries the frequencies of $U$ below $\pi / z$, attenuated by $\hat h$.

The terms $m \neq 0$ carry frequencies above $\pi / z$, folded. An ideal prefilter would have $\hat h = 1$ below $\pi / z$ and $\hat h = 0$ above.

### 4.2 Three measures of the defects

::: def
[Definition 4.3 — Aliasing, blur and ringing of a prefilter]{.tag} For a one-dimensional prefilter $h$ with $\int h = 1$ and $\hat h \in L^2$, and a factor $z$:

-   the **aliasing** is the share of the energy of filtered white noise that lies beyond the new Nyquist frequency and will fold back,
    $$
    \mathcal{A}(h) = \frac{\int_{|\xi| > \pi / z} |\hat h(\xi)|^2\, d\xi}{\int_{\mathbb{R}} |\hat h(\xi)|^2\, d\xi} ;
    $$
-   the **blur** is the mean loss of energy over the frequencies that the coarse grid can carry,
    $$
    \mathcal{B}(h) = \frac{z}{2\pi} \int_{|\xi| \le \pi / z} \big( 1 - |\hat h(\xi)|^2 \big)\, d\xi ;
    $$
-   the **ringing** is the overshoot of the step response $S(x) = \int_{-\infty}^x h$,
    $$
    \mathcal{R}(h) = \max\Big( \sup_x S(x) - 1,\ -\inf_x S(x),\ 0 \Big) .
    $$
:::

The three numbers are dimensionless and lie in $[0, 1]$ for reasonable filters. A filter with $h \ge 0$ has a non-decreasing step response with values in $[0, 1]$, so it has no ringing at all.

### 4.3 The ideal low-pass filter and the Gibbs overshoot

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.4 — The ideal filter rings by 9 %]{.tag} The ideal low-pass prefilter $h(x) = \frac{1}{z} \mathrm{sinc}(x / z)$ has $\mathcal{A} = 0$ and $\mathcal{B} = 0$, and its ringing does not depend on $z$:
$$
\mathcal{R}(h) = \frac{1}{\pi}\, \mathrm{Si}(\pi) - \frac12 \approx 0.0895, \qquad \mathrm{Si}(t) = \int_0^t \frac{\sin s}{s}\, ds .
$$

::: proof
By the table of [ch. 0.1](#ch0) and the dilation rule, $\hat h = \mathbf{1}_{[-\pi/z,\, \pi/z]}$, which gives $\mathcal{A} = \mathcal{B} = 0$.

The change of variables $t = \pi s / z$ in the step response gives
$$
S(x) = \frac12 + \frac{1}{\pi} \mathrm{Si}\Big( \frac{\pi x}{z} \Big) .
$$

The function $\mathrm{Si}$ is odd. Its critical points are the zeros of $\sin t / t$, at $t = j\pi$, and between two of them it changes by the area of one lobe of $\sin t / t$. These areas alternate in sign and decrease in size, so the global maximum of $\mathrm{Si}$ is reached at $t = \pi$.

Hence $\sup S = \frac12 + \mathrm{Si}(\pi)/\pi \approx 1.0895$, reached at $x = z$; by symmetry, $\inf S = -0.0895$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

This is the Gibbs phenomenon. Reducing the factor $z$ narrows the oscillations but never lowers them: every sharp edge of an image reduced with the ideal filter is surrounded by ripples of 9 % of its contrast. Exercise 10 adds a second obstruction: a filter with compact support cannot have $\hat h = 0$ on a whole interval, so zero aliasing needs an infinitely extended kernel.

### 4.4 No escape without ringing

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.5 — Ringing-free prefilters trade blur against aliasing]{.tag} Let $h \ge 0$ with $\int h = 1$. For every frequency $\xi$,
$$
1 - \mathrm{Re}\, \hat h(2\xi) \le 4 \big( 1 - \mathrm{Re}\, \hat h(\xi) \big) .
$$

Consequently, suppose that the prefilter barely blurs the band of the coarse grid: $\mathrm{Re}\, \hat h(\xi) \ge 1 - \varepsilon$ for $|\xi| \le \pi / z$. Then the whole octave above the new Nyquist frequency passes almost unattenuated:
$$
\mathrm{Re}\, \hat h(\xi) \ge 1 - 4 \varepsilon \quad \text{for all } |\xi| \le 2\pi / z .
$$

::: proof
Since $\int h = 1$ and $h$ is real,
$$
1 - \mathrm{Re}\, \hat h(\xi) = \int h(x) \big( 1 - \cos(x\xi) \big)\, dx .
$$

For every real $a$,
$$
1 - \cos 2a = 2 \sin^2 a = 2 (1 - \cos a)(1 + \cos a) \le 4 (1 - \cos a) .
$$

Apply this with $a = x \xi$ and integrate against $h(x)\, dx$. The weight $h$ is non-negative, so the inequality is preserved; this is where the absence of ringing is used.

For the consequence, write any $|\xi'| \le 2\pi / z$ as $\xi' = 2\xi$ with $|\xi| \le \pi / z$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key result — no ringing, no free lunch]{.tag}
$$
h \ge 0,\ \int h = 1 \ \Longrightarrow\ 1 - \mathrm{Re}\, \hat h(2\xi) \le 4 \big( 1 - \mathrm{Re}\, \hat h(\xi) \big)
$$
:::

The constant 4 cannot be improved: for a Gaussian, the ratio of the two sides tends to 1 as $\xi \to 0$. The theorem is the mathematical content of the trade-off of the syllabus. A filter without ringing that keeps the band within $\varepsilon$ passes the next octave within $4\varepsilon$, which then folds. To remove aliasing one must either blur — a wide Gaussian — or accept negative lobes and therefore ringing.

### 4.5 The trade-off in numbers

**Code 4.6 — Measuring prefilters for $z = 2$.** The integrals of Definition 4.3 are computed on a fine frequency grid, and the ringing of the ideal filter by the formula of Proposition 4.4.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.special import sici

z = 2.0                                          # reduction factor
xi = np.linspace(-80, 80, 800001)                # angular frequencies
x = np.linspace(-40, 40, 160001)                 # positions, in fine pixels

def aliasing_blur(H):
    E = np.abs(H)**2
    band = np.abs(xi) <= np.pi / z
    alias = E[~band].sum() / E.sum()             # energy that will fold back
    blur = (z / (2 * np.pi)) * np.sum(1 - E[band]) * (xi[1] - xi[0])
    return alias, blur

rows = []
for c in [0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0]:                   # Gaussian, sigma = c z
    rows.append((f"Gaussian sigma = {c} z", np.exp(-(c * z)**2 * xi**2 / 2), 0.0))
rows.append(("box of width z", np.sinc(z * xi / (2 * np.pi)), 0.0))
step = 0.5 + sici(np.pi * x / z)[0] / np.pi      # step response of the ideal filter
rows.append(("ideal low-pass", (np.abs(xi) <= np.pi / z) * 1.0, step.max() - 1))
print(f"{'prefilter':24s} aliasing   blur  ringing")
for name, H, ring in rows:
    a, b = aliasing_blur(H)
    print(f"{name:24s} {a:8.4f} {b:6.3f} {ring:8.4f}")
```

| Prefilter ($z = 2$) | Aliasing $\mathcal{A}$ | Blur $\mathcal{B}$ | Ringing $\mathcal{R}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gaussian, $\sigma = 0.3 z$ | 0.183 | 0.231 | 0 |
| Gaussian, $\sigma = 0.5 z$ | 0.026 | 0.451 | 0 |
| Gaussian, $\sigma = 0.8 z$ | 0.0004 | 0.647 | 0 |
| Gaussian, $\sigma = 1.0 z$ | $< 10^{-4}$ | 0.718 | 0 |
| box of width $z$ (pixel binning) | 0.223 | 0.226 | 0 |
| ideal low-pass | 0 | 0 | 0.0895 |

Each row sits on one side of the triangle. The Gaussian family slides from aliasing to blur as $\sigma$ grows; the common choice $\sigma \approx 0.8 z$ makes aliasing negligible but blurs noticeably. Averaging $z \times z$ blocks — what binning sensors and many resizing routines do — is the worst compromise: it blurs as much as a Gaussian of width $0.3z$ and aliases more. The ideal filter removes both but rings. Windowed sinc kernels, such as the Lanczos kernels, sit in between, with small negative lobes and small ringing.

### 4.6 Reduction algorithms in practice

-   **Fourier cropping** keeps the central frequencies of the DFT: the ideal low-pass filter on the periodic model. It has no aliasing but rings, and it should be applied to the periodic component of [ch. 2.5](#ch2) so that the border jump does not ring as well.
-   **Gaussian filtering then subsampling** with $\sigma \approx 0.8 z$ has no ringing, almost no aliasing and visible blur. It is the standard choice for scale-space pyramids.
-   **Block averaging** is cheap but aliases, as the table shows.
-   **Least-squares spline reduction** projects the spline model of the fine image on the coarser spline space (Unser, Aldroubi and Eden, 1995); it sits between the Gaussian and the ideal filter.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.7 — Fourier zoom and reduction are inverse to each other]{.tag} Let $M$ be odd and $z \ge 1$ an integer. Let $Z_z$ be the Fourier zoom of Proposition 2.6, from $\mathbb{R}^M$ to $\mathbb{R}^{zM}$.

Let $R_z$ be the Fourier reduction, which keeps the coefficients $|p| \le (M-1)/2$ of a signal of length $zM$, divides them by $z$, and inverts a DFT of size $M$. Then
$$
R_z \circ Z_z = \mathrm{Id}_{\mathbb{R}^M},
$$
and $Z_z \circ R_z$ is the ideal low-pass filter on $\mathbb{R}^{zM}$, an orthogonal projection.

::: proof
By construction, the DFT of $Z_z u$ is $z \hat u_p$ for $|p| \le (M-1)/2$ and zero elsewhere. The reduction divides these coefficients by $z$ and drops the zeros, which gives back $\hat u$.

Conversely, $Z_z R_z w$ keeps the low coefficients of $w$ and zeroes the others. This is a multiplication by an indicator in an orthogonal basis, hence an orthogonal projection. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

**Code 4.8 — Reducing a zone plate.** A zone plate $\cos(\alpha r^2)$ has a local frequency $2\alpha r$ that grows with the radius. Reduced by $z = 2$, its outer ring, with local frequency above the new Nyquist limit, should disappear, while its centre, well inside the band, should keep its contrast (RMS $0.707$).

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import ndimage

n, z = 256, 2
y, x = np.mgrid[0:n, 0:n] - n / 2
r = np.hypot(x, y)
alpha = np.pi / n                             # local frequency 2*alpha*r = pi at r = n/2
u = np.cos(alpha * r**2) * (r < 0.48 * n)     # zone plate, cut before the fine Nyquist

def fourier_reduce(u, z):
    """Keep the central (n/z)^2 DFT coefficients (ideal low-pass + subsampling)."""
    m = u.shape[0] // z
    U = np.fft.fftshift(np.fft.fft2(u))
    c = u.shape[0] // 2
    V = U[c - m // 2:c + m // 2, c - m // 2:c + m // 2].copy()
    V[0, :] = 0; V[:, 0] = 0                  # drop the (ambiguous) Nyquist row/column
    return np.fft.ifft2(np.fft.ifftshift(V)).real / z**2

out = {
    "naive subsampling": u[::z, ::z],
    "Gaussian sigma=0.8z": ndimage.gaussian_filter(u, 0.8 * z, mode="wrap")[::z, ::z],
    "Fourier cropping": fourier_reduce(u, z),
}
rc = r[::z, ::z]                              # radius of the coarse samples (fine units)
outer = (rc > 80) & (rc < 115)                # local frequency above the coarse Nyquist
inner = rc < 40                               # local frequency well inside the band
for name, v in out.items():
    print(f"{name:20s} RMS outer ring {np.sqrt(np.mean(v[outer]**2)):.3f}   "
          f"RMS inner disc {np.sqrt(np.mean(v[inner]**2)):.3f}")
```

| Method | RMS in the outer ring (ideal: 0) | RMS in the centre (ideal: 0.707) | Defect |
|---|---|---|---|
| naive subsampling | 0.705 | 0.714 | aliasing: false rings at full contrast |
| Gaussian, $\sigma = 0.8 z$ | 0.002 | 0.432 | blur: 39 % of the contrast lost |
| Fourier cropping | 0.105 | 0.727 | ringing |

The ringing of Fourier cropping is especially visible here. For a chirp, frequency and position are tied, so cutting the spectrum at $\pi / z$ cuts the pattern sharply at the radius where its local frequency crosses that value, $r = 64$. The sinc tail of that cut oscillates across the outer ring.

::: recap
[Key takeaways — chapter 4]{.tag}

-   Reduction by $z$ keeps the frequencies below $\pi / z$; those above fold back unless the prefilter removes them.
-   Aliasing, blur and ringing are measured by the three quantities $\mathcal{A}$, $\mathcal{B}$, $\mathcal{R}$ of Definition 4.3.
